title: A cell type-aware framework for nominating non-coding variants in Mendelian regulatory disorders
abstract: Unsolved Mendelian cases often lack obvious pathogenic coding variants, suggesting potential non-coding etiologies. Here, we present a single cell multi-omic framework integrating embryonic mouse chromatin accessibility, histone modification, and gene expression assays to discover cranial motor neuron (cMN) cis-regulatory elements and subsequently nominate candidate non-coding variants in the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders (CCDDs), a set of Mendelian disorders altering cMN development. We generated single cell epigenomic profiles for ~86,000 cMNs and related cell types, identifying ~250,000 accessible regulatory elements with cognate gene predictions for ~145,000 putative enhancers. Seventy-five percent of elements (44 of 59) validated in an in vivo transgenic reporter assay, demonstrating that single cell accessibility is a strong predictor of enhancer activity. Applying our cMN atlas to 899 whole genome sequences from 270 genetically unsolved CCDD pedigrees, we achieved significant reduction in our variant search space and nominated candidate variants predicted to regulate known CCDD disease genes MAFB, PHOX2A, CHN1, and EBF3 - as well as new candidates in recurrently mutated enhancers through peak- and gene-centric allelic aggregation. This work provides novel non-coding variant discoveries of relevance to CCDDs and a generalizable framework for nominating non-coding variants of potentially high functional impact in other Mendelian disorders.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This preprint has already been published in a peer-reviewed journal and is beginning to register downstream scholarly use. The record shows one citation so far, along with four documented reuse events, suggesting early but concrete uptake of the framework for non-coding variant nomination in Mendelian regulatory disorders.

Full narrative

A cell type-aware framework for nominating non-coding variants in Mendelian regulatory disorders addresses a central challenge in unresolved Mendelian disease: the absence of obvious pathogenic coding variants. The study introduces a single-cell multi-omic strategy that integrates embryonic mouse chromatin accessibility, histone modification, and gene expression to identify cranial motor neuron cis-regulatory elements and prioritize candidate non-coding variants in congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders. Conceptually, the work sits at the intersection of epigenomics, enhancer biology, and computational genetics, with a clear translational aim.

The strongest signal in the record is publication continuity: the preprint was subsequently published as a peer-reviewed article, indicating that the work moved from posted content into the journal literature. That transition is an important marker of validation and visibility, particularly for a methods-oriented study that depends on multi-omic integration and cell type-specific interpretation.

Scholarly uptake is still early, but it is real. OpenAlex records one citation, and the citing work appears in Nature in 2025. The citing article focuses on enhancer mutagenesis and shares thematic ground with this preprint’s emphasis on regulatory variation, which suggests that the framework is being noticed within adjacent enhancer and chromatin research rather than remaining isolated within a single disease niche.

Beyond formal citation, the record shows four downstream reuse events, including article-level reuse and biomedical mentions in Europe PMC. That combination points to limited but multidimensional circulation: the paper is being referenced in the scholarly literature and surfaced in biomedical indexing contexts. Because the citation base is still very small, the impact profile should be read as emerging rather than established.

Public and social attention appears quiet in the available record, and no platform-specific discussion is documented here. Even so, the article’s trajectory is notable for a translational genomics preprint: it has already crossed into the journal literature, attracted an early citation from a high-profile venue, and generated indexed reuse signals that support its relevance to studies of gene regulation and Mendelian disease.
